issue: Quantitative claim is wrong by a factor of ten. The bullet prints 'extreme sparsity (16/86 ~ 1.8% expert activation)'. 16/86 = 0.18605 = 18.6%, not 1.8%. The printed fraction and the printed percentage are mutually exclusive, and the percentage is load-bearing: the sentence uses it to argue that the memory-bound EP decision is made against total rather than active parameters, and the bullet's closing claim about an 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' rests on the sparsity magnitude.
evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2 ('How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE models at extreme sparsity?'). Recomputation: 16 / 86 = 0.1860465; x100 = 18.60%. To yield ~1.8% the denominator must be ~889 (16/896 = 1.786%), which contradicts the '512 experts' printed two clauses earlier. The same bullet prints 'routes 1e1 of 512 experts' - '1e1' is not a well-formed count (10 in scientific notation, or a mangled '16'/'10') - so neither the numerator nor the denominator of the sparsity fraction can be recovered from the page. 'Kimi 10qB' is likewise a malformed parameter count. Note the operator is '~', so the defect is not a rounding quibble: 18.6% vs 1.8% is a factor of 10, far outside any rounding bound.
acceptance_test: Recover the active-expert count, total-expert count and activated/total parameter split from the cited primary sources ([1P] arXiv 2606.24653 / 2607.24653 and the HF model card). Print one self-consistent triple (active / total = percentage) with correct rounding. Delete '1e1' and '10qB' or replace them with well-formed numerals. Then re-derive the sentence: if the corrected sparsity is ~18.6%, the 'extreme sparsity' framing and the 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' argument must be re-argued, not merely re-digitised.

The bullet contains '[1P]: arXiv 2606.24653; Qwen3-8-Flash-Next routes 1e1 of 512 experts (128B total / 6B active) [1P]: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.' twice - once at the head of the bullet and again immediately after '...increasingly central to serving large MoE fleets'.
evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2. First copy: 'arXiv 2606.24653 ... Qwen3-8-Flash-Next ... HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'. Second copy: 'arXiv 2607.24653 ... Qwen3-8-Flash-Next ... HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'. The copies differ in the arXiv month component (2606 vs 2607) and in the model name spelling ('Qwen3-8-Flash-Next' vs 'Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'), so this is not a clean copy-paste of one string - it is two independently edited variants of the same citation, at least one of which is wrong. The duplication also breaks the sentence: '...large MoE fleets [1P]: arXiv ... . The architecture this changes the serving calculus:' leaves a citation stranded between the clause it was supposed to support and the clause that follows.
acceptance_test: Delete the duplicated citation block and retain exactly one. Verify against the primary source that (a) the arXiv identifier is correct (2606.24653 or 2607.24653, not both), (b) the model name is spelled identically in the citation and in the prose, and (c) the [1P] label binds the clause it supports rather than being repeated. Confirm the bullet reads as one continuous argument with no citation between 'fleets' and 'The architecture'.

issue: The green encoding is given two different semantics on the same page: the legend defines green as 'admission event (backfill)' (an instant), while the in-figure annotation under the continuous panel reads 'new sequences (green) snap into free slots' (a duration — a sequence occupying the slot). The drawn green strips have nonzero width, i.e., they depict admitted sequences in flight, not point events.
evidence: Legend row at top of figure: swatch + 'admission event (backfill)'. Annotation below right panel: 'new sequences (green) snap into free slots'. Green strips in the right panel are wide blocks interleaved between blue blocks, not zero-width markers.
acceptance_test: Legend label and in-figure annotation assign the same referent to green (e.g., legend reads 'newly admitted sequence (backfill)'), or the strips are redrawn as zero-width markers consistent with 'event'. Re-render and confirm both labels match.

issue: The legend defines green as 'admission event (backfill)', but the in-figure annotation says 'new sequences (green) snap into freed slots.' The new sequences are drawn blue; green marks only the admission event. This conflates the event with the sequence and can mislead readers about what continuous batching backfills.
evidence: Legend: 'admission event (backfill)' with green swatch. Bottom-right annotation: 'new sequences (green) snap into freed slots.' The blue bars after each green stripe are the new sequences.
acceptance_test: Change the annotation to 'new sequences enter at green admission events' (or recolor the new sequences green and update the legend). A reader should be able to state that green marks when a slot is refilled, not the sequence itself.

issue: The legend distinguishes 'sequence in flight' (blue solid) from 'admission event' (green solid) by color alone. In grayscale the two solid swatches may be hard to distinguish, and the figure has no grayscale note. The thin green stripes are visually different from the blue bars, but the legend does not encode that shape difference.
evidence: Legend uses a blue solid square for sequence and a green solid square for admission event; no hatch/pattern or grayscale note is present.
acceptance_test: Add a pattern/hatch or explicit label to the admission-event legend, or add a grayscale note explaining the shape distinction. Verify the legend remains unambiguous in grayscale print.

figure: Figure 11.1 (Discrete vs continuous batching, Orca-style slot diagram)
issue: The bottom in-figure annotation 'new sequences (green) snap into freed slots' conflicts with both the legend and the drawing. The legend defines green as 'admission event (backfill)' (a thin one-step tick), and in the right (continuous) panel every green mark is a thin tick sitting between two blue 'sequence in flight' blocks; the new sequence's actual decode is the blue block that follows the tick. Calling the green 'new sequences' lets a reader infer that the green tick IS the new sequence (i.e., that a backfilled sequence occupies only one step), which is false.
evidence: Top legend: green hatched swatch = 'admission event (backfill)'; blue solid = 'sequence in flight'. Right panel rows are of the form [blue][green tick][blue][green tick][blue]. Bottom green annotation: 'new sequences (green) snap into freed slots'.
acceptance_test: Reword the bottom annotation to match the legend and the drawing, e.g. 'a freed slot is backfilled at the green admission tick; the new sequence then runs as the following blue block'. After the change, no reader can conclude from the figure that a backfilled sequence's decode is the green tick.

issue: Border style varies across the four boxes (1 solid, 2 dotted, 3 dash-dot, 4 dashed) but the caption defines only one style: 'dashed border = not in the canonical baseline'. Because one style is explicitly made meaningful, a reader can reasonably search for meaning in the dotted and dash-dot styles of boxes 2 and 3 and find none — an unexplained visual variable.
evidence: Caption: '...resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border = not in the canonical baseline)'. Rendered boxes: 1 solid purple border, 2 dotted red border, 3 dash-dot green border, 4 dashed orange border. No caption or in-figure note explains styles for boxes 1–3.
acceptance_test: Either all four boxes share one border style except box 4 (dashed), or the caption/in-figure note states that border styles for boxes 1–3 are decorative and only 'dashed' carries meaning. Re-render and confirm no undefined border style appears.

issue: The caption says 'dashed border = not in the canonical baseline,' but box 2 also has a non-solid (dotted) border and the figure has no in-figure border-style legend. A reader may infer that box 2 is also outside the canonical baseline, or may not notice which border style carries the meaning.
evidence: Box 1 solid purple, box 2 red dotted, box 3 green dash-dot, box 4 orange dashed. Caption only explains the dashed border for box 4.
acceptance_test: Add a small 'beyond canonical baseline' tag to box 4, or state in the caption that only the orange dashed border carries that meaning. Verify the distinction at print size.

figure: Figure 11.2 (Serving = four separable concerns, not a stack)
issue: Border style is used to encode membership in the canonical baseline, but the encoding is contradicted by the drawing. The caption states 'the canonical baseline uses the first three' and then attaches the rule '(dashed border = not in the canonical baseline)' to resource specialization (box 4). Yet only box 1 has a solid border; box 2 (STATE MANAGEMENT) has a dashed border and box 3 (REUSE) a dash-dot border. A reader applying the caption's rule would misclassify boxes 2 and 3 as outside the baseline, even though the caption says they are in it.
evidence: Caption: '...the canonical baseline uses the first three; resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border = not in the canonical baseline; see "When to Disaggregate", §11.3).' Drawing: box 1 = solid purple border; box 2 = dashed red border; box 3 = dash-dot green border; box 4 = dashed orange border.
acceptance_test: Make border style encode baseline membership consistently: solid border on the three in-baseline concerns (1, 2, 3) and a dashed border only on the out-of-baseline one (4); OR delete the parenthetical 'dashed border = not in the canonical baseline' and instead put an explicit 'not in canonical baseline' tag on box 4. After the change, no reader can infer from border style that box 2 or box 3 is outside the baseline.

figure: FIGURE 11.2 — 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' (2×2 box grid: 1 Request scheduling / 2 State management / 3 Reuse / 4 Resource specialization)
issue: The figure's border-style encoding contradicts the caption's own legend. The caption states: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. That makes dashed border = 'not in the canonical baseline'. But in the rendered figure, boxes 2 (State management) and 3 (Reuse) are ALSO drawn with dashed borders, while box 1 (Request scheduling) is the only solid-bordered box. Under the caption's stated convention, the figure therefore asserts that state management and reuse are excluded from the canonical baseline — the exact opposite of the caption's sentence and of the surrounding chapter (Ch. 11 repeatedly treats PagedAttention and prefix caching as part of the canonical baseline). There is no legend anywhere on the page to disambiguate the border styles, so the reader has no way to resolve the conflict.
evidence: Rendered page 212 (printed 192): box 1 border = solid purple; box 2 = dashed red; box 3 = dashed green; box 4 = dashed orange. Caption text on the same page: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. Only one of the three dashed boxes is explained by the caption; the other two are unexplained and semantically wrong under the caption's rule. Cross-check with printed page 191 (PDF 211), which describes PagedAttention/prefix caching as active mechanisms of the canonical 640 GB node baseline.
root_cause: The figure was authored with 'dashed = distinct/independent concern' (a stylistic device) while the caption repurposed 'dashed' as 'dashed = excluded from canonical baseline'. Two incompatible meanings were assigned to one visual channel.
correction: Pick one meaning for border style and make the figure and caption agree. Preferred: solid border for the three concerns present in the canonical baseline (1, 2, 3) and dashed for 4 only, plus a one-line legend inside the figure ('dashed = not in the canonical baseline; see § 11.3'). If the intended distinction was instead 'solid = scheduling, dashed = the other three', then rewrite the caption clause to say so explicitly and remove the '(dashed border)' parenthetical from the canonical-baseline sentence.
acceptance_test: Render the page and confirm: (a) exactly one box carries the 'not in canonical baseline' border style, and it is box 4; (b) a legend or caption clause states the border-style meaning unambiguously; (c) no reader can reach the conclusion 'PagedAttention and prefix caching are not in the canonical baseline' from the figure alone.

issue: The caption's central claim is that the four concerns 'interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency', and it gives a concrete coupling example ('prefix caching under aggressive continuous batching: cached prefixes and the live batch's pages draw on the same 640 GB KV pool, so reuse needs headroom'). The figure, however, draws four fully disconnected boxes with no arrows, no shared resource, and no coupling annotation. A reader who takes the diagram at face value learns 'four independent, non-interacting components' — which is the opposite of the caption's first clause and is the more consequential misconception, because the coupling (shared KV pool) is exactly what determines whether the four dials can be set independently in practice.
evidence: Rendered page 212: no connectors of any kind between boxes 1–4; the only shared object mentioned in the caption (the 640 GB KV pool) appears nowhere in the drawing. Title 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' reinforces the 'independent' reading.
root_cause: The figure was designed to make the 'not a stack' point (no vertical ordering) and over-corrected into 'no relations at all', losing the interaction the caption asserts.
correction: Add a minimal interaction cue without implying a stack: e.g. a single dashed, non-directional connector or a shared '640 GB KV pool' band beneath boxes 2 and 3 labelled 'shared KV pool → reuse needs headroom', plus a small annotation on the 1→2 edge ('batching pressure → KV residency'). Keep the boxes unordered (no arrows forming a chain). Alternatively, retitle to 'Serving = four concerns, not a stack — but they interact' and let the caption carry the coupling.
acceptance_test: A reader shown only the figure (caption hidden) can state both (a) that the four concerns are not ordered as a stack and (b) that at least one pair shares a constrained resource and therefore cannot be tuned fully independently.

issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak. The four boxes use hue alone to differentiate the concerns: purple (1), red (2), green (3), orange (4). In grayscale, red and orange collapse to nearly the same mid-gray, and green to a similar mid-gray; the only non-color differentiator is border style, which — per FIG-11.2-01 — is itself ambiguous and identical for boxes 2, 3 and 4. The italic 'e.g.' sub-labels are drawn in light tints of the same hues (light red, light green, light orange), which lose further contrast in grayscale and at the small size used. The book must remain interpretable in grayscale and for color-vision-deficient readers.
evidence: Rendered page 212 at 150 dpi: boxes 2/3/4 are visually near-identical in stroke weight and dash pattern, differing only by hue; the sub-label text is noticeably lower-contrast than the box titles.
root_cause: Color was used as the primary categorical channel with no redundant (shape/pattern/label) encoding, and the one redundant channel available (border style) was overloaded with a conflicting meaning.
correction: Add a redundant non-color channel: distinct border patterns per concern (solid / long-dash / dotted / double-line) or a small numeral badge plus a short axis label, and darken the 'e.g.' sub-labels to the same hue as their box titles (or to a neutral dark gray). Keep hue as a tertiary cue only.
acceptance_test: Convert the page to grayscale and confirm all four boxes remain individually identifiable by a non-color cue, and that every 'e.g.' sub-label remains legible at 100% print size.

issue: Two small semantic/pedagogical points. (a) The boxes are numbered 1–4 in reading order, which implies a sequence or precedence even though the title and caption insist the concerns are 'not a stack' and are addressed 'in any order'; the numbering is the only element in the drawing that suggests ordering. (b) The caption's closing italic paragraph states the actual intellectual payload — 'request scheduling exchanges latency for utilization, state management exchanges memory capacity for concurrency, reuse avoids re-prefill FLOPs, and resource specialization splits two compute/memory regimes into two pools' — but none of these trade-offs is encoded in the figure, so the figure carries the least informative content of the pair.
evidence: Rendered page 212: numerals '1 ·', '2 ·', '3 ·', '4 ·' precede the box titles; no trade-off text appears inside any box.
root_cause: Numbering was used for reference convenience; the trade-off dimension was left entirely to the caption.
correction: Either drop the numerals (or replace them with non-ordinal tags such as 'SCHED'/'STATE'/'REUSE'/'SPEC') so no ordering is implied, or add a one-line trade-off under each 'e.g.' label (e.g. 'latency ↔ utilization'). If the trade-offs are added, the figure becomes the primary carrier of the caption's key insight and the caption can be shortened.
acceptance_test: Figure alone conveys, for each of the four concerns, the mechanism and the resource it trades; no visual element implies an ordering among the four.

issue: Page composition: the figure plus its long caption (roughly 20 lines, including a separate italic paragraph) ends about three-quarters of the way down the page, leaving a large empty band at the bottom of a page that is otherwise a single figure-and-caption unit. The caption is also unusually long relative to the figure it annotates — the figure is four boxes with short labels, while the caption carries the mechanism choices, the interaction example, the canonical-baseline rule, the cross-reference to § 11.3, and a separate trade-off paragraph.
evidence: Rendered page 212: bottom ~25% of the text block is blank; caption occupies more vertical space than the diagram.
root_cause: Caption was written to stand alone as a mini-essay, and the figure was not sized to carry more of that content.
correction: Move the trade-off content into the figure (see FIG-11.2-04) and compress the caption to: what the figure shows, the canonical-baseline rule, and the § 11.3 pointer. This both shortens the caption and lets the figure be enlarged to fill the page, improving label legibility.
acceptance_test: Caption reduced to ≤ 12 lines; figure enlarged so that the smallest label is ≥ 8 pt at final print size; no page in the chapter ends with more than ~20% trailing whitespace.
